title: Machine learning uncovers four new extracellular contractile injection-system toxins
summary: An XGBoost classifier trained on genomic and biochemical features prioritized eCIS-associated toxins from bacterial and archaeal genomes. Four candidates, EAT14–17, were experimentally shown to be toxic in bacterial and/or yeast cells; EAT14 also inhibited Rac1/Cdc42-mediated mitogenic signaling in human cells.
ai_technology: XGBoost classifier for extracellular contractile injection-system-associated toxins (EATs)
organization: Hebrew University of Jerusalem; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; collaborators

evidence.tested: Four candidates, EAT14–17, were experimentally shown to be toxic in bacterial and/or yeast cells; EAT14 also inhibited Rac1/Cdc42-mediated mitogenic signaling in human cells.
evidence.unknown: Four of eight selected candidates were toxic under the tested heterologous-expression assays; the authors report an empirical positive predictive value of 50% for this sample and discuss possible host/compartment mismatch. Toxin delivery by native eCIS and physiological target organisms remain incompletely established. EAT14’s signaling effect was shown in human cells, not as a therapeutic effect.
evidence.ai_role: The classifier used genomic and protein biochemical features to score candidate EAT genes across eCIS-positive microbial genomes. The model narrowed candidates for functional tests; heterologous expression assays validated four previously uncharacterized toxins, with follow-up active-site mutations and a human-cell signaling assay.
